claims.text: Mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering is a viable route for producing bulk refractory high-entropy alloys.
Adding 0.5–1 wt.% Y2O3 nanoparticles to a W–Mo–Ta–Nb–V-based refractory HEA will produce a uniform oxide dispersion.
Dispersion-control measures such as surfactants or modified milling parameters can improve Y2O3 dispersion during mechanical alloying.
Approximately 50 hours of milling followed by SPS at 950–1150 °C is a suitable processing window for the proposed Y2O3-containing refractory HEA.
The proposed processing route will leave nanoscale Y2O3 particles embedded in the HEA matrix.
The Y2O3 particles will remain stable during processing and high-temperature service.
Y2O3 dispersoids will obstruct dislocation motion at high temperature through particle-strengthening and pinning effects.
Y2O3 dispersoids will inhibit grain-boundary movement.
The oxide dispersion will stabilize the refractory HEA microstructure against coarsening.
The oxide dispersion will increase high-temperature yield strength.
The oxide dispersion will increase high-temperature creep resistance.
At approximately 1000 °C, high-temperature yield strength and creep resistance will improve by about 20–30% relative to an otherwise comparable alloy without Y2O3.
The low Y2O3 fraction will have no detrimental effect on alloy density.
The low Y2O3 fraction will preserve room-temperature ductility.
The predicted improvement will hold at approximately 1000 °C under high-strain-rate loading.
Particle coarsening or inhomogeneous Y2O3 dispersion may negate the high-temperature mechanical benefit.

contradictions.description: The stated performance baseline is an HEA without Y2O3, but the falsification experiment compares two groups that both contain Y2O3 and differ only in dispersion-control measures. It therefore does not directly test the predicted improvement relative to the stated baseline.

The prediction specifies a 20–30% improvement, whereas the falsification rule only rejects an improvement below about 15%; a result between 15% and 20% would miss the predicted range without falsifying the hypothesis.
The hypothesis predicts no detrimental density change, but density is not included among the decisive experiment's measurements or falsification criteria.
